groups.title: What the gods give
groups.intro: These signs are the gifts in almost every scene: gods hold them out to the king, and the king asks for them. Learn these first.

groups.title: Names of gods
groups.intro: A god’s name is often written beside or above the figure. These few groups cover most of the Hall.

groups.title: The king’s titles
groups.intro: Small groups of signs that stand in front of the royal names. They tell you a name is coming, and which one.

groups.title: Signs inside royal names
groups.intro: The building blocks of the cartouches in the Hall. With these you can tell the kings apart.

groups.title: Speech and small words
groups.intro: Signs that turn a scene into dialogue: “words spoken”, “I have given”, “you”, “he”. Many are used only for their sound.

groups.title: Protection, people and enemies
groups.intro: Signs for the powers that guard the king, for Egypt’s people, and for its enemies.

groups.title: Time and eternity
groups.intro: Kings asked the gods for endless time. These signs count it.

signs.name: Ankh
signs.why: Gods hold it out to the king, often right up to his nose, giving him the breath of life. In texts it follows the king’s names: “given life”. A king holding one, like Sety I on the south wall, is shown as divine.
signs.where: Everywhere. In the published wall texts of the Hall, “given life” occurs more than 300 times.

citations.locator: The ankh marks Sety I as divine
Frequency of “given life” in the translations

signs.name: Was sceptre
signs.why: A staff with an animal head at the top and a forked foot. Gods carry it as a sign of their power, and grant “dominion” to the king.
signs.where: In gods’ hands in the ritual scenes, and in the phrase “life, stability and dominion”.

signs.name: Djed pillar
signs.why: A pillar with four bars across the top, linked with Osiris. Granting “stability” means the king’s rule will last.
signs.where: In the phrase “life, stability and dominion”, which appears around 200 times in the wall texts.

signs.name: Cone of bread (“give”)
signs.why: A pointed loaf used to write the verb “to give”. It is the first sign of “given life” and of every god’s promise “I have given to you…”.
signs.where: After almost every royal name and in every god’s speech.

signs.name: Offering table
signs.meaning: offering; to be satisfied, at peace
signs.why: A mat with a loaf of bread on it. It means both “offering” and “peace”: a god who receives offerings is satisfied.
signs.where: In offering scenes and in phrases like “in peace”.

signs.name: Sun disk
signs.why: The sun god’s name, and part of almost every royal name in the Hall. Because it is a god’s name, it is written first in a cartouche even when it is spoken last.
signs.where: In every cartouche of Sety I and Ramesses II. On the column photo it opens the name Usermaatre-setepenre.

signs.name: Amun group
signs.why: Three signs spelling Amun’s name by sound: a reed leaf (i), a game board (mn) and a ripple of water (n). Karnak is Amun’s temple, so this group is everywhere, often inside royal names as “beloved of Amun”.
signs.where: In the birth names Ramesses-meryamun and Sety-merenamun, and over figures of Amun-Re.

signs.name: Flag on a pole
signs.why: A cloth flag on a pole, like the flagpoles that once stood in front of temple pylons. It writes the word “god”.
signs.where: In “the good god” before royal names, and in “lord of the gods”.

signs.name: Seated Maat
signs.why: A seated goddess with an ostrich feather on her head. Keeping Maat was the king’s first duty, and many royal names contain her.
signs.where: In the throne names of Sety I (Menmaatre) and Ramesses II (Usermaatre). On the column photo she holds an ankh.

signs.name: Ostrich feather
signs.why: The feather alone can write Maat’s name. Maat wears one on her head; Amun’s crown has two tall plumes.
signs.where: In names and on figures of Maat.

signs.name: Falcon
signs.why: The living king was Horus on earth. A falcon on a palace front (the serekh) introduces the king’s Horus name.
signs.where: Before the king’s Horus name (“Horus: mighty bull…”) and as the god Horus, who purifies the king.

signs.name: Vulture
signs.why: The vulture writes “mother” and the name of Mut, Amun’s wife. A vulture with spread wings over the king is a protecting goddess.
signs.where: Above the king in many scenes, like the one flying over Ramesses II at stop 6.

signs.name: Throne seat and eye
signs.why: A throne seat and an eye write the name of Osiris, god of the dead. A dead king is called “Osiris King …”.
signs.where: In the texts around Sety I’s statue at stop 6 (“Osiris King Menmaatre”).

signs.name: Sedge plant
signs.why: The sedge plant of the south. With the bee it makes the title “King of Upper and Lower Egypt”, which always comes just before the throne name.
signs.where: In front of the first cartouche of a pair.

signs.name: Bee
signs.why: The bee of the north. Sedge and bee together, each with a small loaf (t) under it, read nesu-bity.
signs.where: In front of the throne name, next to the sedge plant.

signs.name: Pintail duck
signs.why: A duck that writes “son”. Duck plus sun disk reads “son of Re”, the title in front of the king’s birth name.
signs.where: Before the second cartouche. On the painted beam, two ducks with sun disks introduce Sety I’s name.

citations.locator: “son of Re” before the birth name

signs.name: Basket
signs.why: A plain basket. On its own it reads “lord”; after a word it means “all”. It appears in “lord of the Two Lands” and “all life”.
signs.where: In front of royal names, and under the rekhyt birds at the column bases.

signs.name: Strip of land
signs.why: A strip of earth with grains of sand. Written twice it means “the Two Lands”: Upper and Lower Egypt.
signs.where: In “lord of the Two Lands”, one of the most common titles in the Hall (about 300 times in the wall texts).

citations.locator: Frequency of “lord of the Two Lands”

signs.name: Hill with rising sun
signs.why: The sun rising over a hill. “Lord of appearances” stands before the birth name: the king appears like the sun.
signs.where: In “lord of appearances” before the second cartouche.

signs.name: Heart and windpipe
signs.why: A heart with the windpipe. “The good god” (netjer nefer) is a standard way to refer to the living king.
signs.where: Before royal names: “the good god Menmaatre”.

signs.name: Cartouche
signs.why: A loop of rope tied at one end, stretched into an oval. It encloses a king’s throne name and birth name.
signs.where: On every wall and column. Ramesses IV’s alone appear thousands of times.

citations.locator: Ramesses IV’s cartouches repeated thousands of times

signs.name: Palace front (serekh)
signs.why: A palace façade with a falcon on top. It frames the king’s Horus name, the oldest of his five names.
signs.where: Ramesses IV added large Horus names at the bases of the central columns.

citations.locator: Ramesses IV’s cartouches and Horus names on the great columns

signs.name: Head of a canine on a staff
signs.why: The head and neck of a dog-like animal. It opens the throne name Usermaatre, used by Ramesses II, Ramesses III and, early on, Ramesses IV.
signs.where: On the column photo, just after the sun disk.

signs.name: Game board
signs.why: A senet game board with its pieces on top, used for the sound men. It is the “Men” in Sety I’s Menmaatre and in Amun’s name.
signs.where: Low in Sety I’s cartouche at stop 6 (marker 6).

signs.name: Adze
signs.why: A carpenter’s adze. “Setep-en-Re” means “chosen of Re”: Ramesses II’s final throne name ends with it.
signs.where: Near the end of Usermaatre-setepenre on the column photo.

signs.name: Hoe
signs.why: A hoe used for the sound mer. “Mery-Amun”, “beloved of Amun”, is part of the birth names of Ramesses II and the throne names of Ramesses III and VI.
signs.where: Inside cartouches, next to the Amun group.

signs.name: Three fox skins
signs.meaning: to be born; to give birth
signs.why: Three animal skins tied together. With the sun disk it spells Ra-mes-su: “Re is the one who bore him”. It is how you recognise any Ramesses.
signs.where: In the birth names of Ramesses I to VI.

signs.name: Folded cloth
signs.why: A folded cloth used for the sound s. It follows the fox skins in the name Ramesses.
signs.where: After the fox skins in Ramesses’ name.

signs.name: Crook
signs.why: The shepherd’s crook carried by kings. Ramesses IV’s later throne name, Heqamaatre (“Re is the ruler of Maat”), uses it instead of user.
signs.where: In Ramesses IV’s cartouches on the columns.

signs.name: Scarab beetle
signs.why: The dung beetle, linked with the rising sun. It appears in throne names such as Horemheb’s Djeserkheperure.
signs.where: In Horemheb’s names on the Second Pylon gateway.

signs.name: Cobra (sound dj)
signs.meaning: the sound dj; first sign of “to speak”
signs.why: A cobra used for its sound. With a hand and a staff it writes djed medu, “words spoken”, which opens every speech.
signs.where: At the start of almost every god’s speech.

signs.name: Staff
signs.why: A walking staff that writes “words”. Look for it near the start of a text column in front of a god.
signs.where: In “words spoken by …” (more than 100 times in the wall texts).

signs.name: Ripple of water
signs.why: A line of water used for the sound n. It also means “to” or “of”: “I have given to you”, “chosen of Re”.
signs.where: Everywhere, including under the adze in setepenre.

signs.name: Basket with handle
signs.why: A basket with a handle, for the sound k. Added to a word it means “you”: the god is speaking to the king.
signs.where: At the end of “I have given to you”.

signs.name: Horned viper
signs.why: A horned viper, for the sound f. Added to a word it means “he” or “his”.
signs.where: In phrases like “his father”.

signs.name: Owl
signs.why: An owl seen face-on, for the sound m. As a word it means “in” or “as”.
signs.where: Very common in running texts.

signs.name: Mouth
signs.why: A mouth, for the sound r.
signs.where: Very common in running texts.

signs.name: Small loaf
signs.meaning: the sound t; marks a feminine word
signs.why: A small half-round loaf for the sound t. It sits under the sedge and the bee in nesu-bity.
signs.where: Under many signs, including in the king’s title.

signs.name: Seated man
signs.meaning: “I, me”; marks a word about a man
signs.why: A seated man. After a verb in a speech it can mean “I”; at the end of a word it shows the word is about a person.
signs.where: At the end of words for people and in some speeches.

signs.name: Rearing cobra (uraeus)
signs.why: The cobra rearing on the king’s brow, believed to spit fire at his enemies. As a sign it stands for the goddess who protects him.
signs.where: On royal crowns, and in the friezes of cobras near the tops of the great columns.

signs.name: Eye of Horus
signs.why: The eye of Horus with falcon markings, a sign of healing and protection.
signs.where: In ritual scenes and on amulets.

signs.name: Shen ring
signs.why: A loop of rope with no beginning or end. Vultures and falcons often hold one in their claws over the king. The cartouche is a stretched shen ring.
signs.where: In the claws of vultures over the king.

signs.name: Lapwing (rekhyt)
signs.why: A lapwing with its wings pinned. At the bases of the small columns, rekhyt birds sit on baskets (“all”) and raise their arms to Ramesses II’s names: all the people worship the king. It told visitors they were allowed in this part of the temple, even if they could not read.
signs.where: At the bases of many of the 122 smaller columns.

citations.locator: Rekhyt birds on neb signs at the column bases

signs.name: Bow
signs.why: A bow. The “Nine Bows” are Egypt’s traditional enemies. Bound captives appear under the king’s feet and on the outer battle walls.
signs.where: On the outer walls and in triumph scenes.

signs.name: God Heh with raised arms
signs.why: A kneeling god holding up his arms. He stands for an uncountable number: “millions of years” of reign.
signs.where: On the year staves in the scene next to stop 6 (B93).

citations.locator: Plate 49 (B93), p. 99: year staves with ḥḥ.w “millions”

signs.name: Palm rib
signs.why: A palm rib with notches: the tally stick for counting years. Gods hold long notched staves to write down the king’s years of reign.
signs.where: In the year-staves scene next to stop 6 (B93).

signs.name: Jubilee pavilion
signs.why: A double pavilion with two thrones, used for the jubilee festival that renewed a king’s power. Gods promise the king “millions of jubilees”.
signs.where: On the year staves and in gods’ speeches.
